extracted.intended_audience: business owners, marketers, designers and non-designers creating infographics
extracted.subtask_description: Practical best-practice guidance for creating single-page or short-format infographics aimed at marketing, lead-generation, and audience engagement. Focuses on visual hierarchy, data visualization choice, typography, color, dimensions, mobile responsiveness, and footer/attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to one main point
rubrics_metrics.description: An infographic is meant to visually illustrate a set of data or supporting arguments for one main point; it isn’t the place for a deep dive or multiple tangents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on a single topic and avoid different interpretations, side arguments or tangents. Choose topics interesting to and valuable for your target audience to draw leads. Brainstorm topics with a specific audience in mind. Use tools (e.g., Visme AI text generator) to create concise main points, outlines, shorten text, and section information effectively. Keep the infographic concise, ideally a single page, to maintain engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let visuals do the talking
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographics should rely on graphic elements to present information; text should be mostly supplementary so the graphic still makes sense with most text removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagery related to the topic to make visuals memorable. Maintain consistency in design elements (e.g., if you use line icons, use them throughout). Include appropriate combinations of visual/text elements (subheader, body copy, quote, CTA, stats, icons, diagrams, photography, data visualizations). Test whether the graphic conveys the gist with minimal text. Consider AI image generation for unique visuals when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include appropriate data visualizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the data visualization type that makes the most sense for your data or message (charts, diagrams, graphs, icons, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are many visualization types (over 44 referenced). Use radial elements for percentages, Venn diagrams to compare, circle/stacked charts to compare numbers, flowcharts for hierarchies or chronological data, line/scatter graphs for data over time. Determine visualization type by first obtaining and understanding your data. Use editor tools to test charts, tables, widgets, maps and other visualizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your flow make sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the visual reading order is obvious so viewers know which order to read data and supporting arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place elements in a logical order or use lines/arrows/visual indicators to direct the eye. Use numbering, clear separations (different colors or blocks) between sections, or arrows to guide movement. Avoid layouts where the reader is unsure where to look next; use visual cues to prevent confusion or overwhelm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose 2–3 complementary fonts
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit fonts to two or three complementary faces (one may be an accent) and avoid decorative or script fonts except at very large sizes (e.g., headers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer combinations like serif/sans-serif or mix classifications for contrast. Don’t pair two fonts from the same classification. Use contrasting sizes (e.g., 36pt header with 16–18pt body) and contrasting weights (bold for headings, regular for body). Optionally use different fonts per text level (one for headers, one for subheadings, one for body) and avoid switching fonts within the same level to prevent clutter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a basic color scheme (2–3 colors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stick to a simple color palette—generally two or three colors—unless using an acceptable multi-shade or full-spectrum approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions include monochromatic schemes (different shades of one color) or spectrum/rainbow styles. Use company branding colors where possible for consistency and brand recognition; if brand has one color, pick complementary shades. Match colors to content (e.g., strawberries -> pinks/reds) or draw inspiration from nature. Use palette tools (Visme, Coolors, Color Hunt, Design Seeds, Paletton) to generate cohesive schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider infographic dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose dimensions appropriate to how much information you need, where you’ll share the infographic, and how the audience consumes content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common format is long vertical, but choose square for Instagram, horizontal for slide decks/presentations, or other aspect ratios as needed. Ask: how much info, how will it be shared, who is the audience, do you want it to be shareable, is it part of a longer project? Use the visualization of common dimensions to pick the right one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make it mobile friendly
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your infographic is readable and usable on mobile devices as well as desktop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the KISS principle (Keep It Simple). Avoid tiny text that forces excessive zooming. Make infographics responsive (build as responsive landing pages rather than long static JPGs) so content reorganizes to fit screen sizes. Separate into snackable chunks or create alternate versions (e.g., Instagram carousel, slideshow). Use live links (Visme) to preserve resolution, animations, interactivity, live data updates, and to access analytics on viewership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include correct footer information
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide source attribution and contact/branding details in the footer of the infographic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List exact sources for data and statistics to show credibility. Include company name, logo, URL, and social icons. Add a call-to-action (purchase, learn more, donate, etc.). Use dynamic fields to keep footer information consistent across multiple assets and make updates easily. Giving credit and making it easy to find the creator builds trust and drives traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of a strong infographic
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong infographic has clear visual hierarchy, relevant data, concise text and engaging design; information should be easily digestible and logically organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure data is represented with a logical flow and the layout remains organized and concise. The design should be visually appealing while prioritizing readability and information clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common pitfalls (what not to do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common anti-patterns include clutter, excessive text, unclear visuals, inconsistent style, and overloading the infographic with unnecessary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit information to essentials, use brief captions, prevent confusion by maintaining consistent styles and clear visuals. Avoid mixing too many font types, colors, or graphic styles that make the design look messy. If something can’t be explained simply, reconsider its inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead with a captivating headline
rubrics_metrics.description: The first element on your infographic should be a captivating and informative headline to capture attention and set the tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The headline should immediately communicate the infographic’s main point and entice viewers to continue reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep infographics to a single page when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally an infographic should be kept to a single page to maintain viewer engagement and simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concise one-page format encourages quick comprehension and reduces risk of overwhelming the audience. If more space is needed, consider chunking into multiple shareable pieces (carousel, slideshow) or creating an alternate, longer version.
